Tidak lagi didorong oleh rasa ingin tahu eksperimental atau sebagai tindakan pemberontakan semata, tapi sebagai ekspresi alami dari cinta, kenyamanan, dan kebutuhan koneksi yang mendalam di tengah kerasnya kehidupan. Momen-momen keintiman itu—berpelukan di bawah selimut kulit hewan rakitan saat malam dingin, berbagi kehangatan tubuh setelah seharian bekerja keras, atau sekadar sentuhan lembut penuh pengertian—menjadi pengingat konstan akan kemanusiaan mereka, menjadi sumber kekuatan dan "hormon bahagia" yang membantu mereka melewati hari-hari sulit. Mereka tidak lagi mengejar "orgasme dahsyat" seperti dalam teks, melainkan menemukan kepuasan mendalam dalam keseluruhan proses kebersamaan fisik dan emosional itu.

Tentu saja, bayangan Neo-Jakarta tidak sepenuhnya hilang. Sesekali, melalui perangkat komunikasi radio jarak jauh yang diperbaiki Lyra, mereka menangkap siaran berita terfragmentasi dari kota. Mereka mendengar tentang dampak jangka panjang logic bomb mereka—gangguan sistemik minor yang terus muncul, peningkatan level ketidakpercayaan publik pada algoritma tertentu, dan rumor tentang gerakan bawah tanah baru yang terinspirasi oleh "Anomali Kembar" (julukan sistem untuk Lyra dan Orion). Kabar ini menimbulkan perasaan campur aduk: ada kepuasan karena tindakan mereka ternyata berdampak, tapi juga ada rasa tanggung jawab dan kekhawatiran akan nasib orang-orang yang mungkin terinspirasi oleh mereka.

Buku kulit usang itu masih mereka simpan dengan baik. Isinya kini terasa seperti teman lama, sumber kebijaksanaan yang relevan dalam konteks baru mereka. Mereka tidak lagi hanya membacanya, tapi menghidupinya. Mereka bahkan mulai berbagi beberapa konsepnya secara hati-hati dengan anggota komunitas mereka yang tampak terbuka—tentang pentingnya keseimbangan logika dan emosi, tentang kekuatan komunikasi jujur dalam menyelesaikan konflik komunal.

Suatu senja, setelah setahun hidup di Zona Bebas, Lyra dan Orion duduk di puncak sebuah bukit kecil, memandang matahari terbenam yang sesungguhnya. Langit barat terbakar dengan warna jingga, merah muda, dan ungu yang liar dan tak terduga—spektrum warna yang tidak pernah ada dalam palet terkontrol Neo-Jakarta. Pemandangan itu begitu indah hingga menyakitkan.
"Apakah kau pernah menyesal, Orion?" tanya Lyra pelan, menyandarkan kepalanya di bahu Orion.

Orion terdiam sejenak, menatap cakrawala yang berwarna-warni itu. "Menyesali kenyamanan dan keamanan semu di atas sana? Tidak pernah," jawabnya mantap. "Menyesali rasa sakit dan ketakutan yang kita alami? Ya, kadang-kadang. Tapi…" ia menoleh pada Lyra, matanya memantulkan cahaya senja, "…aku tidak akan menukarnya dengan apapun. Karena di sini," ia menggenggam tangan Lyra erat, "aku menemukan diriku sendiri. Dan aku menemukanmu. Benar-benar menemukanmu."
Lyra tersenyum, senyum tulus yang mencapai matanya. "Aku juga," bisiknya. "Hidup di sini sulit, tidak pasti. Tapi ini… nyata. Kita bebas untuk merasa, untuk memilih jalan kita sendiri."

Mereka tahu masa depan masih penuh tantangan. Membangun kehidupan baru di dunia yang liar ini membutuhkan kerja keras, ketahanan, dan keberuntungan. Mungkin suatu hari nanti sistem Neo-Jakarta akan mencoba memperluas jangkauannya lagi, atau mungkin konflik internal dalam komunitas Zona Bebas akan muncul. Ketidakpastian adalah bagian dari kebebasan baru mereka.

Tapi saat matahari akhirnya tenggelam di balik pegunungan jauh, meninggalkan langit yang dihiasi ribuan bintang berkelip (bukan proyeksi data), Lyra dan Orion tidak lagi merasa takut. Mereka saling berpegangan tangan, merasakan kehangatan satu sama lain, merasakan kekuatan tenang yang lahir dari cinta yang teruji dan kebebasan yang diraih dengan susah payah. Fajar mungkin telah lama berlalu, tapi cahaya merah jambu harapan dan cinta kini bersinar konstan di hati mereka, menerangi jalan mereka ke depan, apapun yang mungkin menanti. Mereka siap menghadapi hari esok, bersama-sama, sebagai partner sejati, sebagai jiwa yang akhirnya merdeka.

chapters.heading: Gema yang Tersisa
paragraphs: Lima tahun telah berlalu sejak Lyra dan Orion menemukan perlindungan di Zona Bebas. Lima tahun membangun kehidupan baru dari nol, di bawah langit yang sesungguhnya dan di luar jangkauan langsung algoritma Neo-Jakarta. Kehidupan tidaklah mudah. Musim kemarau yang panjang menguji persediaan air mereka, badai dahsyat sesekali merusak pondok-pondok sederhana komunitas, dan ancaman dari satwa liar atau kelompok penjarah lain yang juga menghuni Zona Bebas selalu ada. Namun, di tengah kesulitan itu, tumbuh kehidupan yang berbeda—kehidupan yang kaya akan tekstur, emosi, dan koneksi manusiawi yang otentik.

Lyra tidak lagi hanya seorang teknisi data. Ia telah menjadi salah satu pilar komunitas kecil mereka. Selain menjaga dan mengembangkan sistem teknologi darurat komunitas (komunikasi radio, pemurnian air, energi terbarukan skala kecil), ia juga menjadi seorang guru. Di sebuah bangunan kayu sederhana yang berfungsi sebagai sekolah komunitas, ia mengajar anak-anak—anak-anak yang lahir bebas dari indoktrinasi logika sistem—tentang sains dasar, matematika, tapi juga, secara hati-hati, tentang sejarah yang dihapus dan konsep-konsep dari Kode Leluhur: tentang pentingnya empati, komunikasi jujur, dan menghargai perasaan. Ia menemukan kegembiraan yang mendalam saat melihat mata anak-anak itu berbinar karena keingintahuan, bukan karena data yang terpampang di layar.

Orion telah sepenuhnya melepaskan sisa-sisa identitas Alpha-nya. Ia menjadi salah satu pemburu dan pelindung utama komunitas, keterampilannya membaca alam dan strategi bertahan hidup kini terasah tajam. Namun, ia juga menemukan panggilan sejatinya dalam seni. Ukiran-ukiran kayunya, yang menangkap keindahan liar Zona Bebas sekaligus kerapuhan dan kekuatan jiwa manusia, menjadi sangat dihargai oleh komunitas, berfungsi sebagai pengingat visual akan nilai-nilai yang mereka perjuangkan. Ia juga menjadi pendongeng ulung, menceritakan kembali kisah-kisah dari teks kuno (yang telah mereka terjemahkan bersama Lyra) atau legenda para Penyimpan Ingatan di sekitar api unggun pada malam hari, menjaga agar sejarah dan harapan tetap hidup.

Hubungan Lyra dan Orion telah mencapai kedalaman dan kematangan yang tenang. Badai besar yang mereka lalui bersama telah mematri jiwa mereka menjadi satu kesatuan yang tak terpisahkan. Gairah masa muda mungkin telah bertransformasi menjadi bara api yang hangat dan stabil, namun keintiman emosional, fisik, dan spiritual mereka semakin mengakar kuat. Mereka adalah partner sejati dalam setiap aspek kehidupan. Mereka belajar menavigasi perselisihan kecil dengan komunikasi terbuka dan empati yang telah mereka latih. Mereka saling memberikan ruang untuk tumbuh sebagai individu, sambil tetap menjadi pelabuhan aman bagi satu sama lain. Keintiman fisik mereka kini lebih merupakan perayaan hening atas kebersamaan, kenyamanan, dan cinta yang teruji waktu, sebuah ritual harian yang menguatkan ikatan mereka.

Buku kulit usang itu kini disimpan dengan hati-hati di tempat terhormat di perpustakaan kecil komunitas, bersama dengan salinan digital yang Lyra buat dan arsip datacrystal para Penyimpan Ingatan. Isinya tidak lagi dianggap sebagai rahasia berbahaya, tapi sebagai warisan berharga. Konsep-konsepnya—tentang keseimbangan logika dan emosi, pentingnya hubungan holistik, kekuatan kerentanan—perlahan mulai diintegrasikan ke dalam etos komunitas, diajarkan kepada generasi baru, menjadi dasar bagi cara hidup alternatif yang mereka coba bangun. Mereka tidak bertujuan menciptakan utopia—Zona Bebas terlalu keras untuk itu—tapi mereka berusaha membangun masyarakat yang lebih manusiawi, yang menghargai perasaan sama tingginya dengan kelangsungan hidup.

Sesekali, kabar dari Neo-Jakarta masih sampai kepada mereka melalui jalur komunikasi rahasia dengan sisa-sisa jaringan Penyimpan Ingatan di dalam kota. Gambaran yang muncul campur aduk. Di satu sisi, sistem tampaknya telah berhasil menekan gejolak terbuka pasca insiden sub-stasiun. Propaganda tentang "Anomali Kembar" yang berbahaya terus digaungkan. Kontrol pengawasan diperketat, algoritma diperbarui untuk mendeteksi deviasi emosional dengan lebih canggih. Neo-Jakarta, di permukaan, kembali ke efisiensi dinginnya.

Namun, di sisi lain, gema tindakan mereka tetap terasa. Ada laporan tentang meningkatnya permintaan sesi "konseling emosional" (meskipun masih dalam kerangka korektif sistem), tentang munculnya karya seni atau musik bawah tanah yang secara samar mengekspresikan kerinduan atau ketidakpuasan, tentang beberapa pejabat level Beta atau bahkan Alpha yang diam-diam mempertanyakan rigiditas sistem setelah melihat retakan yang sempat terbuka. Kisah Lyra dan Orion, meskipun dipelintir oleh propaganda, telah menjadi legenda urban terlarang, simbol samar bahwa perlawanan terhadap mesin logika itu mungkin, bahwa ada sesuatu di luar sana. Benih keraguan telah tertanam, meskipun mungkin membutuhkan waktu bergenerasi-generasi untuk tumbuh.

Lyra dan Orion telah memilih untuk tidak memiliki anak sendiri. Keputusan itu sulit, tapi mereka merasa dunia yang mereka tinggali masih terlalu tidak pasti, dan mereka tidak ingin memaksakan beban warisan perlawanan mereka pada generasi berikutnya. Namun, mereka mencurahkan cinta dan perhatian mereka pada anak-anak komunitas, mencoba membekali mereka dengan pengetahuan dan kebijaksanaan untuk memilih jalan mereka sendiri kelak.

Suatu sore yang cerah, setelah hujan badai semalam membersihkan udara, Lyra dan Orion berjalan menyusuri tepi hutan di dekat pemukiman mereka. Mereka baru saja selesai membantu memperbaiki sistem irigasi darurat untuk kebun komunal. Tangan mereka bertaut dengan nyaman, sebuah kebiasaan yang kini terasa sama alaminya seperti bernapas.

Mereka berhenti di sebuah tebing kecil yang menghadap lembah hijau yang luas. Pelangi ganda yang spektakuler—fenomena alam yang liar dan tak terduga—membentang di langit setelah badai. Pemandangan itu begitu indah, begitu berbeda dari proyeksi data terkontrol Neo-Jakarta.

1: Neo-Jakarta breathed in a rhythm of cold efficiency and metronomic precision. The sky above rarely displayed natural blue; more often it was covered by a thin layer of atmospheric filter projecting daily schedules, air quality indexes, or communal energy efficiency data in a controlled spectrum of pastel colors. There were no lazily drifting clouds or dramatic orange sunsets. Here, even natural phenomena submitted to optimization.

Towering from reclamation land forcibly seized from Jakarta Bay a century ago, Neo-Jakarta's skyscrapers gleamed like blades of obsidian and chromium piercing the sky filter. Their designs were uniform, geometric, prioritizing function above all aesthetics considered wasteful. Building facades were coated with smart solar panels adjusting their transparency based on sunlight intensity and district energy needs. There were no messy balconies with laundry lines or wild flower pots disturbing the clean lines of architecture. Every inch of space was designed for maximum productivity.

The streets below were no longer arenas of honking chaos and human traffic jams as in the ancient archives of Old Jakarta. Multi-level lanes flowed with autonomous personal and communal transport pods moving silently in programmed trajectories, controlled by the Central Transportation Algorithm (APT). There were no human drivers, no angry shouts, only the soft hiss of electric motors and a nearly perfect flow of vehicles, minimal pauses, minimal friction. Pedestrians, if any, moved on sterile elevated walkways connecting buildings, their steps uniform, their gazes straight ahead, focused on data interfaces floating thinly before their eyes or projected from smart contact lenses.

In Neo-Jakarta in the year 2142, logic was god, efficiency was its sacred mantra. Emotions — especially those considered negative or unproductive like deep sadness, overflowing anger, excessive anxiety, even uncontrolled euphoria — were viewed as primitive artifacts, a bug in the human operating system that must be suppressed, managed, or if necessary, eliminated through scheduled behavioral therapy or mild pharmacological intervention regulated by the Communal Mental Health Algorithm (AKMK). Booming free laughter or sobbing tears in public spaces would immediately trigger a notification to the nearest Emotion Compliance Officer. Physical intimacy in public — holding hands too long, an embrace considered too tight, let alone a kiss — was considered a waste of emotional energy and a disturbance to social order. Everything was recorded, analyzed, becoming part of every individual's social compliance score.

Human relationships also didn't escape this cold calculation. Marriage or Long-Term Partnership (KJP), as the official term went, was no longer based on ancient inefficient concepts like “love at first sight” or “spontaneous attraction.” Everything was regulated by the Genetic and Social Compatibility Algorithm (AKGS). From adolescent age, every individual's biometric data, psychological profile (continuously updated by AKMK), caste status, and economic contribution potential were entered into the system. AKGS would then calculate and present a list of potential partner candidates with the highest KJP success probability — measured from social stability, potential for genetically superior offspring, and minimal potential for emotional conflict.

First meetings were arranged in controlled environments, facilitated by AI mediators. Initial interaction focused on data exchange and logical compatibility analysis. If both parties agreed to continue, the KJP would be officially registered, often without involving obsolete ceremonies considered inefficient. The main purpose of KJP was social stability and optimal population sustainability. Concepts like “passion,” “longing of the soul,” or holistic sexual satisfaction discussed in forgotten literature were considered sentimental fiction or, worse, hormonal disorders that must be managed. Physical intimacy in KJP was functional, scheduled, and often procreation-oriented according to district quotas. Appreciating the uniqueness of a partner's body as something beautiful and arousing was an absurd concept.

Amid this cold and measured social order, Lyra lived her days. Identification Unit: 734-Gamma-Lyra. Caste: Data Technician Level 3 (Gamma). KJP Status: Not Yet Initiated (Awaiting Next Cycle AKGS Computation Results). Living in Communal Apartment Block District 7, a housing efficiency tower on the outskirts of Neo-Jakarta's technology industrial zone.

Lyra's living space was a perfect reflection of her world: a capsule unit of 15 square meters, minimalist to the bone. Sterile white walls, multifunctional furniture folded neatly into the wall when not in use, an integrated personal data terminal displaying daily schedules and nutritional intake recommended by the Personal Health Algorithm (AKP). No photos, no personal trinkets, no physical books or artworks — all considered unnecessary clutter-adders. The only “decorative” element was a small terrarium containing softly glowing synthetic moss in the room's corner, an incentive reward for achieving work efficiency targets three consecutive quarters.

Morning began exactly at 05:30 Neo-Jakarta Standard Time (SWNJ) when the interface on the wall blinked softly, waking Lyra with a controlled dawn light simulation and low-frequency sonic alarm sound designed for optimal transition from sleep to waking state. There was no snooze button. Delay was considered inefficiency. After a quick and measured self-hygiene routine in the private sanitation booth (water and soap usage monitored), Lyra donned her work uniform: a neutral gray jumpsuit made of smart-fabric regulating body temperature and monitoring basic vital signs.

Breakfast was not a leisurely ritual. Lyra swallowed homogeneous nutrition paste dispensed from the wall dispenser, its composition precisely adjusted by AKP based on her daily calorie and micronutrient needs. Its taste was neutral; its purpose was fuel, not enjoyment. While eating, she absorbed the morning news summary and that day's task priorities through her smart contact lenses. That day's headlines: “District 4 Logistics Network Optimization Reaches 98.7% Efficiency,” “Public Sentiment Analysis Shows 0.3% Increase in Satisfaction With AKGS Performance,” “Weather Warning: Potential Light Acid Rain in Northern Sector 14:00-15:00 SWNJ.” Everything was data, numbers, percentages. There were no human stories, no emotional drama.
At 06:15 SWNJ, Lyra was already inside the communal transport pod gliding silently toward District 7 Data Processing Center (PPD-7), her workplace.

That 15-minute journey she spent reviewing data logs from the previous night shift, preparing her brain for the massive flow of information she would soon face. Inside the pod, other passengers sat in the same silence, their eyes fixed on their respective personal interfaces, social interaction minimal. There was no small talk, no friendly smiles. Communication happened only if necessary for functional coordination.
Lyra's job was analyzing and maintaining a specific segment of the Social Compliance Algorithm (AKS), one of the core algorithms supporting Neo-Jakarta's order.

Her task was identifying anomalies, potential behavioral deviations, or collective emotional fluctuations that could disturb system efficiency. She stared at the raw data flowing swiftly on the multi-dimensional holographic screen before her — communal heartbeat graphs, linguistic patterns from encrypted public communications, anonymous biochemical data from sanitation systems, even micro-expression data captured by public sensors — seeking patterns, seeking outliers.

Lyra was very good at her job. Her brain was trained to think logically, analytically, and objectively. She could process extraordinarily large volumes of data with high speed and accuracy. Her own emotions were conditioned to remain flat, stable. She rarely felt significant surges of happiness or sadness. If she felt slightly tired or unfocused, she would request a cognitive support supplement dosage adjustment from AKP, or schedule a brief relaxation session in the sonic meditation pod available at the office. Feelings were considered variables to be managed, not experienced. She understood that individual emotional stability was the key to system stability as a whole. She accepted that logic without question.

However, today, something strange happened. While analyzing historical data from the previous century's public communications archive — a routine task to retrain the sentiment recognition algorithm — she found an anomaly. Not a statistical data anomaly, but an audio fragment missed by standard filtering. That archive came from the pre-Optimization era, the era of Old Jakarta that was chaotic and inefficient by Neo-Jakarta standards.

In that low-quality audio fragment, the sound of laughter could be heard. Not the polite and controlled laughter sometimes heard in Neo-Jakarta, but free laughter, booming, full of pure happiness that felt so… inefficient. That laughter was contagious, even through an obsolete recording. For a confusing fraction of a second, Lyra felt something foreign in her chest, a strange tickling sensation rising to her throat. The muscles at the corners of her lips unconsciously pulled slightly upward.

She froze. That unexpected physical reaction felt disturbing. Illogical. She immediately accessed her personal biometric log. Heart rate slightly increased. Pleasure-related neurotransmitter activity detected at low levels. Not dangerous, but clearly a deviation from her emotional baseline.

With quick and efficient movements, Lyra marked that audio fragment as corrupted data, deleted it from the algorithm's training set, and sent an automatic notification to the Archive Maintenance Division. She then activated a brief emotional calibration protocol through her interface — a series of visual patterns and audio frequencies designed to return her mental status to optimal neutral condition. Within seconds, the strange sensation in her chest disappeared. Logic took over again. That was just corrupted data, an artifact from an irrational past. Irrelevant.

However, though she quickly suppressed and ignored that small incident, a faint residue remained in her subconscious. Like a small glitch in a perfect program, a microscopic question not yet articulated: why did that sound of such inefficient laughter feel… pleasant? That question was dangerous, illogical. She pushed it far away. There were still thousands of terabytes of other anomalous data awaiting her analysis today. Efficiency must be maintained.

Lyra returned focus to the holographic screen before her, her fingers dancing nimbly over the virtual console, her brain again unraveling complex patterns in the ocean of data. Outside PPD-7's tightly sealed windows, transport pods kept gliding in their precision ballet beneath the neutral filter sky. Life in Neo-Jakarta ran as usual, regulated by cold and tireless algorithms. Lyra, data technician 734-Gamma, was one small but important cog in that giant machine, functioning according to program, logical, efficient. At least, for now. That spark of anomaly in the archive data earlier, though deleted, might have planted the first seed of something she hadn't anticipated at all inside her neatly controlled operating system. A seed awaiting the next trigger to begin germinating.
2: Far above District 7's efficiency towers inhabited by Gamma technicians like Lyra, Neo-Jakarta's Alpha Sector gleamed with cold and calculated luxury. This was where Orion spent most of his work cycles. Identification Unit: 12-Alpha-Orion. Caste: Executive Official Level 2 (Alpha). KJP Status: In Algorithmic Exploration Process (Top 3 Candidates with Compatibility Score >92%).

Orion's apartment at the Central Tower's Peak was the antithesis of Lyra's minimalist capsule, but ironically, equally sterile in its own way. The rooms were spacious, with ceiling-height panorama windows presenting the city's geometric view stretching flawlessly below. The furniture was made of exotic materials — solidified liquid metal, genetically engineered wood — with avant-garde designs more resembling art installations than functional seats or tables. Lighting was regulated by Orion's personal AI, adjusting intensity and color spectrum based on his biological schedule and desired productivity level. The air was filtered in layers, ionized, and given a neutral aroma designed to stimulate cognitive focus. Everything was perfect, everything optimal, everything… hollow.

Orion's morning began an hour earlier than Lyra's, at 04:30 SWNJ, with a cognitive stimulation session and high-precision virtual physical exercise in his private fitness room. His breakfast was also nutrition paste, though perhaps with more diverse synthetic flavor variants than those available to the Gamma caste. His work involved high-level data analysis, oversight of algorithm policy implementation, and scheduled interaction with other Alpha officials or delegations from other districts.

Orion was a perfect product of the Neo-Jakarta system. Intelligent, ambitious, logical, and his emotions well controlled. He understood and (mostly) believed in the principles of efficiency and logic supporting his world. He saw the chaos and irrationality in Old Jakarta's archive data as proof of the current order's superiority. He accepted algorithmic matchmaking as the most rational method to ensure social stability and species continuity.

However, lately, fine cracks had begun appearing in the facade of his sturdy conviction. Not logical doubt — statistical data clearly showed declining crime rates, increased life expectancy, and economic stability since the Optimization era. That doubt was more… visceral. A vague feeling of disturbing emptiness that couldn't be explained by algorithms or neutralized by scheduled sonic meditation sessions.

He felt it when interacting with the three top KJP candidates presented by AKGS. Alpha women who were intelligent, genetically healthy, and socially compatible with him. Their interactions were efficient, polite, focused on data exchange and long-term goal analysis. But there was no… spark. No illogical heartbeat, no impulsive desire to touch or simply gaze longer. Everything felt like a very important business transaction, not a meeting of two souls. The concept of “chemistry” or “emotional bond” perhaps discussed in those forgotten texts was entirely absent. Orion tried to ignore this feeling, labeling it as an irrational expectation caused by consumption of ancient fiction narratives accidentally exposed to him as a teenager. But that feeling persisted, settling like sediment at the bottom of his consciousness.

He also felt it when overseeing implementation of the Social Compliance Algorithm (AKS) in the lower sectors. Seeing how the system with merciless efficiency flagged individuals showing even the smallest emotional deviation, scheduling them for “correction.” He knew it was necessary for stability, for the greater good. But sometimes, seeing the biometric data of a Gamma individual flagged for showing an abnormal oxytocin surge (the bonding and affection hormone) while interacting with their core family unit, Orion felt an illogical sting of discomfort. Must efficiency mean total sterility from human warmth?

A few days later, a routine inspection assignment brought him down from Alpha Sector's sterile heights to the depths of District 7 Data Processing Center (PPD-7). A massive but functional facility where Gamma technicians like Lyra worked tirelessly unraveling the city's ocean of data. Orion didn't like visits to the lower sectors; the air felt denser, the efficiency slightly less optimal, and interaction with the Gamma caste always felt awkward to him. But this inspection was important — there were reports about a persistent anomaly in the pre-Optimization historical data archive segment handled by PPD-7, an anomaly with potential to disturb the accuracy of long-term social prediction algorithms.

When Orion arrived at PPD-7, he was welcomed by the Chief Gamma Technician who bowed respectfully with programmed compliance. The air inside that data center was cold from supercomputer cooling systems, filled with constant humming from thousands of working servers. Rows of Gamma technicians sat before their holographic consoles, their faces illuminated by blue-green data light, their fingers moving quickly, their eyes focused, nearly without expression. Efficient.

The Chief Technician escorted Orion toward the Far Archive Sector, an area with higher security levels in the building's belly. This was where the oldest, most sensitive, and often most “chaotic” data from the Old Jakarta era was stored and occasionally accessed for algorithm recalibration.

“Anomaly detected in Sub-sector 7-Psi, Master Orion,” the Chief Technician reported in a flat tone. “Primarily related to socio-cultural archive data from the mid-21st century. There are several files resistant to standard cleaning protocols and continuing to produce inconsistent sentiment readings. Technician 734-Gamma, Lyra, is conducting deep diagnostic analysis at this time.”

Lyra. Orion remembered that identification unit from the minor incident report a few days ago — the technician who reported corrupted audio data containing laughter. An insignificant coincidence, he thought.

They entered Sub-sector 7-Psi. That room was dimmer than the main work area, server racks containing quantum data storage units towering high on both sides. In the middle of the room, before a special analysis console, sat a Gamma technician — Lyra. She was so focused on the complex data flow before her that she didn't notice Orion and the Chief Technician's arrival behind her.
“Technician Lyra,” called the Chief Technician.

Lyra startled slightly, then quickly rose and gave a standard salute. “Master Orion. Chief Technician.” Her face was neutral, like other Gamma technicians, but Orion caught a brief flash of something in her eyes when she saw Orion — not fear or admiration, more like… controlled curiosity? Or perhaps only a projection of Orion's own feelings.
“Report anomaly status, Technician,” Orion ordered, his voice cold and formal.

Lyra returned to her console. “The anomaly centers on a series of encrypted data files miscategorized as transition-era logistics archives, Master. However, initial analysis shows very different content. Its data structure is unrecognized, its encryption uses an ancient protocol not present in standard databases. I am attempting forced decryption using heuristic algorithms, but the process is very slow and consumes large computational resources.”

She displayed several lines of random code and a complex data structure diagram on the main screen. “There is strong indication that these files were deliberately hidden or protected from standard archive cleaning protocols,” Lyra added, her tone remaining flat yet implying significance.

Orion observed the data on screen with a furrowed brow. His professional curiosity was stirred. Data deliberately hidden from the pre-Optimization era? That was unusual. Standard protocol was to delete or quarantine such data to prevent ideological “contamination.”

“Focus additional computational resources on the decryption process,” Orion ordered the Chief Technician. “I want to see this file's content as soon as possible. Report directly to me if there's a breakthrough.”
“Yes, Master Orion,” the Chief Technician answered.

As Orion was about to turn to leave, something in the corner of Lyra's console drew his attention. Not digital data, but a small physical object lying beside the virtual keyboard. That object appeared like… a book? Not a thin data tablet or flexible scroll, but a book bound in worn leather, with paper that looked yellowed and fragile. The existence of such an analog object at the heart of this ultra-modern data center felt very odd, very out of place.
“What is that, Technician?” Orion asked sharply, pointing toward the book.

Lyra appeared slightly surprised by the question. She hesitated a moment before answering. “This… this is one of the physical artifacts found together with that anomalous data file, Master. Inside a lead-shielded storage container on the same server rack. I haven't had a chance to report it.”

Orion stepped closer, his curiosity now greatly stirred. He gestured for Lyra to move aside. Carefully, as if touching an explosive material, Orion took that old book. Its leather cover felt rough and cracked in his hands. There was no title, only a strange symbol faintly engraved on the front. He opened its first page very carefully.

The paper was fragile, smelling of dust and time. Its writing wasn't standard Neo-Jakarta digital text, but ancient handwriting curving beautifully, using ink that had already faded. Its language… ancient Indonesian, but with vocabulary and style that felt foreign, poetic, full of emotion.
Orion's eyes fixed on the first few sentences on that page:

“…and know, O seeking soul, that the peak of true pleasure isn't merely momentary release of desire, but the meeting of two souls longing for each other, in a dance of vulnerability and total surrender. It is a symphony of passion and unspoken understanding…”

Orion felt a strange sting in his chest, similar to what Lyra might have felt hearing that laughter in the audio archive. These words… so different, so… alive. The concepts of “meeting of souls,” “vulnerability,” “total surrender” were anathema to Neo-Jakarta logic.
He turned the next page with slightly trembling fingers.

“Don't be afraid to open your heart, don't be ashamed to show your fragility. Because precisely there lies your most essential strength. In your partner's gaze that accepts you wholly, without condition, you will find home…”

Orion swallowed. These words seemed to speak directly to the emptiness he felt. He glanced at Lyra standing stiffly a few steps from him. Had this Gamma technician already read this? Her expression was still neutral, but Orion felt he caught a glimmer of the same understanding or shock in her deep eyes.

He turned the page again. This time a rough diagram, a sketch of human anatomy with points marked with strange names and descriptions about “pleasure zones” and “gateways to tremendous orgasm.” Beside it, was written:

“Communication is the key. Speak your desire, listen to her longing. Explore every curve of her body with reverence, appreciate her uniqueness as if she were the most precious treasure map. Foreplay isn't a warm-up, but an act of worship…”

Orion closed that book suddenly, his heart beating illogically. His head felt dizzy from information so contradictory to everything he knew and believed. This book… was dangerous. Very dangerous. Its contents were poison to Neo-Jakarta's social order. This was the kind of knowledge that could awaken the wild and uncontrolled emotions the system had suppressed with such difficulty over centuries. This was thinking that could trigger instability, rebellion.

Standard protocol required him to immediately confiscate this book and related data files, report them as high-level subversive material, and surrender them for immediate destruction. Technician Lyra, as the person who first found them, might have to undergo intensive emotional examination.

But… something held him back. Burning curiosity, which felt stronger than his logical indoctrination. The feeling that this book held answers to the emptiness he felt. And perhaps… perhaps also a spark of distrust toward the system he had all this time served faithfully.

He looked at Lyra again. This time, he was certain he saw something else in that Gamma technician's eyes. Not only curiosity, but also… understanding? Did Lyra also feel the same thing when briefly reading this book or trying to decrypt its digital files?
“Those digital files,” Orion said softly, his voice slightly hoarse, trying to sound calm and authoritative. “Have you succeeded in decrypting part of their contents, Technician?”

Lyra nodded slowly. “A small part, Master. Its contents… similar to this physical text. Descriptions about… emotional connection, physical sensation… things that don't exist in our standard data.” She stopped, as if hesitant to continue. “There is also discussion about… endorphin hormones, oxytocin… as triggers of happiness and bonding produced from… intimate interaction.”
Orion fell silent. Happiness hormones from intimate interaction? That concept was so primitive, so… inefficient. But somehow, felt so appealing.
An impulsive, illogical decision formed in Orion's mind. A decision that could destroy his career, even his life.

“Technician Lyra,” Orion said softly, ensuring only Lyra could hear him, ignoring the Chief Technician standing a few meters behind them. “Stop the forced decryption process. Quarantine these files with the highest security level. Do not report the discovery of this physical book in the official log. Consider this anomaly still under internal investigation by me personally.”

Lyra looked at Orion, her eyes widening slightly with shock hearing an order so violating protocol. But she didn't ask. She only nodded slowly once more. “Yes, Master Orion.” There was a glimmer of silent understanding that seemed to weave between the two of them in that brief moment, amid the cold humming of data servers.

Orion slipped that old book into his slim work bag, his movement quick and hidden. “Continue your other work, Technician,” he said in a formal tone, before turning and walking out of Sub-sector 7-Psi, leaving Lyra alone with her data console and the dangerous secret they had just shared without words.

As Orion returned to Alpha Sector in his private pod, that old book felt burning inside his bag. He knew he had just crossed a boundary he shouldn't have. He was bringing home a time bomb, a forbidden code that could collapse his entire ordered world. But he couldn't restrain himself. The curiosity and emptiness in his heart were too strong. He had to know more. And he felt, somehow, that the Gamma Technician named Lyra was the key to unlocking the secrets of this forbidden text. Their next meeting, he knew, would no longer be official in nature.

Tears flowed down Lyra's and Orion's cheeks. Not tears of sadness or fear, but tears of relief, emotion, and freedom they had just achieved. They had succeeded. They had gotten out of the cage of logic.

They didn't know what awaited them in this Free Zone. There might be new challenges, new dangers. Building a new life from zero wouldn't be easy. But as they stood there, beneath their first genuine dawn light, gazing at an uncertain yet possibility-filled future, they knew one thing: they would face it together.

Lyra rested her head on Orion's shoulder, feeling the sun's warmth on her skin for the first time. Orion embraced her tightly, breathing in the free air deeply. That worn leather book was still stored safely with him, no longer as a forbidden text, but as a reminder of their journey, as a guide toward the new life they would build together — a life based not on cold algorithms, but on the warmth of human connection, on the courage to feel, and on the beauty of pink dawn blooming in their hearts.

Their struggle against the system might not be fully over, its echo might still be felt in Neo-Jakarta. But their personal struggle to find freedom of soul and true love had reached its peak. They had found their new rhythm, a harmony born from the storm, ready to welcome the symphony of new life awaiting ahead.
14: A year had passed since Lyra and Orion stepped out of the darkness of Neo-Jakarta's underground tunnels toward genuine sunlight. A year since they first breathed unfiltered free air, felt wild wind on their faces, and gazed at limitless blue sky undisturbed by communal data projections. The Free Zone, which once was only a legend in the whispers of Memory Keepers and a faint map in an ancient book, was now their reality — a reality that was harsh, unpredictable, yet strangely, liberating.

This place wasn't a utopian paradise. This was a wild landscape not yet fully recovered from the ecological disaster centuries ago, before Neo-Jakarta's Optimization era. Remnants of old civilization — building skeletons swallowed by wild vines, cracked roads becoming seasonal riverbeds — became silent witnesses of a chaotic past. Small isolated communities were scattered across this vast territory, consisting of descendants of those who rejected or fled Neo-Jakarta's control, living in fragile symbiosis with nature that was sometimes cruel. There was no central algorithm, no security guarantee, no nutrition paste distributed. There was only nature's unpredictable cycle — scorching heat, storms, successful planting seasons, difficult famine seasons — and the jungle law of survival.

For Lyra and Orion, adaptation was a brutal yet transformative process. Lyra, whose brain was accustomed to processing terabytes of abstract data, now had to learn to read nature's signs: wind direction, cloud patterns, wild animal tracks. Her technical expertise wasn't entirely useless; it became very valuable in repairing remnants of pre-Optimization technology used by the small community they joined — old solar panels, simple water purification systems, short-range radio communication devices. She found new satisfaction in her real handiwork, repairing something broken with limited components, seeing the results of her work directly help the community's survival. Her logic was now applied to practical problem-solving, no longer to maintaining the efficiency of an oppressive system. She also learned to garden, feeling soil texture in her hands, tending plants from seed to harvest — an “inefficient” process giving her a sense of connection with life's cycle she'd never felt before.

Orion faced a different challenge. All the Alpha attributes that once defined him — status, knowledge of system protocols, strategic analysis ability — were nearly useless here. He had to learn the most basic skills from scratch: hunting with simple tools, building shelter, identifying edible plants, lighting fire without a sonic igniter. At first it felt humiliating and frustrating. There were times he missed the comfort and certainty of his old life, doubting his choice. But every time that doubt appeared, he would look at Lyra — see her resilience and adaptability, see the new light in her eyes that no longer only reflected data — and he would remember why they were doing this.

Gradually, Orion began finding his new rhythm. He realized that his physical strength, once only honed in virtual simulation, turned out to be quite useful in manual work. He found unexpected patience while tracking game or waiting for plants to grow. And most surprisingly, he rediscovered the artistic talent buried since his childhood, before the system suppressed it as unproductive. He began carving driftwood into expressive forms or painting the wild landscapes of the Free Zone using natural pigments he learned from one of the community elders. Art became his way of processing experience, expressing emotions that now flowed freely, and rediscovering his identity beyond the Alpha label.

Their relationship also evolved. Without caste walls, without surveillance pressure, without social masks to wear, they became truly equal, truly partners in the real sense. They relied on each other for daily survival. Lyra relied on Orion's physical strength and calm when facing unexpected danger (like sudden storms or encounters with predatory wildlife). Orion relied on Lyra's analytical intelligence and calm when planning hunts or managing their limited resource supplies.

The principles from that forbidden text were now no longer theory, but their lived practice. “Heart-to-heart communication” happened naturally as they shared fears on cold nights or celebrated small successes finding a new water source. “Vulnerability” was no longer frightening, but became glue when one of them admitted exhaustion or doubt, and the other responded with empathy and support. They learned to apologize sincerely when small disagreements arose from stress, and to forgive quickly, realizing how precious their togetherness was.

Their physical intimacy also found a new rhythm more grounded and satisfying. No longer driven by experimental curiosity or as an act of mere rebellion, but as a natural expression of love, comfort, and the need for deep connection amid life's harshness. Those moments of intimacy — embracing under assembled animal-hide blankets on cold nights, sharing body warmth after a day of hard work, or simply a gentle touch full of understanding — became a constant reminder of their humanity, becoming a source of strength and “happiness hormones” that helped them get through difficult days. They no longer chased “tremendous orgasm” as in the text, but rather found deep satisfaction in the whole process of that physical and emotional togetherness.

Of course, Neo-Jakarta's shadow hadn't fully disappeared. Occasionally, through the long-range radio communication device Lyra repaired, they caught fragmented news broadcasts from the city. They heard about the long-term impact of their logic bomb — minor systemic disruptions that kept appearing, increased levels of public distrust in certain algorithms, and rumors about a new underground movement inspired by the “Twin Anomalies” (the system's nickname for Lyra and Orion). This news raised mixed feelings: there was satisfaction because their actions turned out to have impact, but also a sense of responsibility and worry about the fate of people who might be inspired by them.

They still kept that worn leather book well. Its contents now felt like an old friend, a source of wisdom relevant in their new context. They no longer only read it, but lived it. They even began sharing some of its concepts carefully with members of their community who seemed open — about the importance of balancing logic and emotion, about the power of honest communication in resolving communal conflict.

One dusk, after a year living in the Free Zone, Lyra and Orion sat atop a small hill, watching a genuine sunset. The western sky burned with orange, pink, and purple that were wild and unpredictable — a spectrum of colors that never existed in Neo-Jakarta's controlled palette. That view was so beautiful it hurt.
“Have you ever regretted it, Orion?” Lyra asked softly, resting her head on Orion's shoulder.

Orion fell silent a moment, gazing at that colorful horizon. “Regret the illusory comfort and security up there? Never,” he answered firmly. “Regret the pain and fear we experienced? Yes, sometimes. But…” he turned to Lyra, his eyes reflecting the dusk light, “…I wouldn't trade it for anything. Because here,” he gripped Lyra's hand tightly, “I found myself. And I found you. Truly found you.”
Lyra smiled, a sincere smile reaching her eyes. “Me too,” she whispered. “Life here is hard, uncertain. But this… is real. We're free to feel, to choose our own path.”

They knew the future was still full of challenges. Building a new life in this wild world required hard work, resilience, and luck. Maybe someday the Neo-Jakarta system would try to expand its reach again, or maybe internal conflict within the Free Zone community would emerge. Uncertainty was part of their new freedom.

But as the sun finally set behind distant mountains, leaving a sky decorated with thousands of twinkling stars (not data projections), Lyra and Orion no longer felt afraid. They held each other's hands, feeling each other's warmth, feeling the calm strength born from tested love and hard-won freedom. Dawn might have long passed, but the pink light of hope and love now shone constantly in their hearts, illuminating their path forward, whatever might await. They were ready to face tomorrow, together, as true partners, as souls finally free.
15: Five years had passed since Lyra and Orion found protection in the Free Zone. Five years building a new life from zero, under a genuine sky and beyond the direct reach of Neo-Jakarta's algorithms. Life wasn't easy. Long dry seasons tested their water supplies, powerful storms occasionally damaged the community's simple huts, and threats from wildlife or other scavenger groups also inhabiting the Free Zone were always present. However, amid that difficulty, a different life grew — a life rich in texture, emotion, and authentic human connection.

Lyra was no longer merely a data technician. She had become one of the pillars of their small community. Besides maintaining and developing the community's emergency technology systems (radio communication, water purification, small-scale renewable energy), she also became a teacher. In a simple wooden building functioning as the community school, she taught children — children born free from the system's logic indoctrination — about basic science, mathematics, but also, carefully, about erased history and concepts from the Ancestors' Code: about the importance of empathy, honest communication, and appreciating feelings. She found deep joy seeing those children's eyes gleam with curiosity, not because of data displayed on a screen.

Orion had fully released the remnants of his Alpha identity. He became one of the community's main hunters and protectors, his skills in reading nature and survival strategy now sharply honed. However, he also found his true calling in art. His wood carvings, capturing the wild beauty of the Free Zone as well as the fragility and strength of the human soul, became greatly appreciated by the community, serving as visual reminders of the values they fought for. He also became an accomplished storyteller, retelling stories from the ancient text (which he and Lyra had translated together) or Memory Keeper legends around the campfire at night, keeping history and hope alive.

Lyra and Orion's relationship had reached a calm depth and maturity. The great storm they'd passed through together had forged their souls into one inseparable unity. The passion of youth might have transformed into a warm and stable ember, but their emotional, physical, and spiritual intimacy grew increasingly deeply rooted. They were true partners in every aspect of life. They learned to navigate small disagreements with the open communication and empathy they had practiced. They gave each other room to grow as individuals, while remaining a safe harbor for each other. Their physical intimacy was now more a silent celebration of togetherness, comfort, and time-tested love, a daily ritual strengthening their bond.

That worn leather book was now carefully stored in a place of honor in the community's small library, along with the digital copy Lyra made and the Memory Keepers' datacrystal archives. Its contents were no longer considered a dangerous secret, but a precious legacy. Its concepts — about the balance of logic and emotion, the importance of holistic relationships, the power of vulnerability — slowly began being integrated into the community's ethos, taught to the new generation, becoming a foundation for the alternative way of life they tried to build. They didn't aim to create a utopia — the Free Zone was too harsh for that — but they strove to build a more humane society, one that valued feelings as highly as survival.

Occasionally, news from Neo-Jakarta still reached them through secret communication channels with remnants of the Memory Keepers' network inside the city. The picture that emerged was mixed. On one hand, the system appeared to have succeeded in suppressing open turmoil after the sub-station incident. Propaganda about the dangerous “Twin Anomalies” kept being echoed. Surveillance control was tightened, algorithms updated to detect emotional deviation more sophisticatedly. Neo-Jakarta, on the surface, returned to its cold efficiency.

However, on the other hand, the echo of their action remained felt. There were reports about increasing demand for “emotional counseling” sessions (though still within the system's corrective framework), about the emergence of underground art or music vaguely expressing longing or dissatisfaction, about several Beta-level or even Alpha officials quietly questioning the system's rigidity after seeing the cracks that had briefly opened. Lyra and Orion's story, though twisted by propaganda, had become a forbidden urban legend, a vague symbol that resistance against the logic machine was possible, that there was something out there. Seeds of doubt had been planted, though they might require generations to grow.

Lyra and Orion had chosen not to have children of their own. That decision was difficult, but they felt the world they inhabited was still too uncertain, and they didn't want to impose the burden of their legacy of resistance on the next generation. However, they poured their love and attention onto the community's children, trying to equip them with knowledge and wisdom to choose their own path someday.

One bright afternoon, after last night's storm cleansed the air, Lyra and Orion walked along the forest edge near their settlement. They had just finished helping repair the emergency irrigation system for the communal garden. Their hands were clasped comfortably, a habit that now felt as natural as breathing.

They stopped at a small cliff overlooking a vast green valley. A spectacular double rainbow — a wild and unpredictable natural phenomenon — stretched across the sky after the storm. That view was so beautiful, so different from Neo-Jakarta's controlled data projections.
“Sometimes I still can't believe we're really here,” Lyra whispered, resting her head on Orion's shoulder. “Living like this.”
Orion embraced her. “We chose this path, Lyra,” he answered gently. “With all its difficulties, this is the life we chose. A real life.”
“Do you think… Neo-Jakarta will change someday?” Lyra asked, voicing a question that often appeared in their minds. “Did our sacrifice… mean something there?”

Orion gazed at the distant horizon, where the unseen Neo-Jakarta lay. “I don't know for certain,” he admitted honestly. “A system like that is very strong, very adept at adapting. It might not collapse anytime soon.” He paused a moment. “But we have proven that the human soul cannot be fully programmed or extinguished. We proved that love and connection are real, and stronger than even the coldest algorithm. That echo… that echo will remain, Lyra. Perhaps not heard loudly, but it will keep resonating.”

He turned to Lyra, his eyes full of love and calm certainty. “And most importantly,” he continued, “we found our own freedom. Here.” He pointed to their hearts. “Freedom to feel, to choose, to love each other unconditionally. Isn't that our greatest victory?”

Lyra smiled, tears of emotion pooling in her eyes. Orion was right. The war against the system might still be long and its outcome uncertain. But their internal war, the war to reclaim their humanity, they had won.

They stood there a long time, at that cliff's edge, watching the rainbow slowly fade as the sun began to descend. Their hands still tightly clasped, a symbol of their unbreakable bond. They were two anomalies, two fugitives, two souls who found their way home in each other's embrace, in the wild world they now called home. The pink dawn light might have long passed, but the warmth of its rays now lived eternally within them, illuminating their path full of challenges yet also full of meaning, day by day, together. Their legacy wasn't a great revolution, but a gentle yet persistent whisper about the power of love and freedom of soul that couldn't be silenced by logic however cold. And for them, that was more than enough.
